title: Five EU countries plan a "return hub" in Rwanda for rejected asylum seekers
seoTitle: EU Rwanda return hub: Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece, Netherlands
dek: Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced on 16 November that they aim to open a centre in Rwanda in 2027 for people whose asylum claims have been rejected and appeals exhausted. Nothing has been signed; rights groups oppose it.
happened: Meeting in Vienna on 16 November, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced, together with Rwanda, that they aim to set up a "return hub" there for people under enforceable removal orders, including rejected asylum seekers who are not Rwandan. Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the aim is for the first centre to open next year. People sent there could stay and integrate in Rwanda, return voluntarily to their home country, or move to another country where they can legally live. The five governments would pay the hub's direct costs; no total cost or number of people has been given. The European Parliament voted in June to allow member states, alone or in small groups, to set up such centres outside the EU. The EU recorded 669,365 first-time asylum applications in 2025, about 45% of which are approved on average.

sides.says: Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said: "I think this will be a game changer" and "The most important number is the number that we will never see." German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the plan covers only people who have been through the asylum process and exhausted their appeals, and is "incomparable" with the UK's scrapped Rwanda plan. Dutch Deputy Prime Minister Bart van den Brink said Rwanda was chosen for its "considerable experience" in receiving migrants. European officials say the hubs would follow European and international law.
Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said arrivals would get a "second chance", that the UN refugee agency would be involved and that "there will be an independent monitoring mechanism".

UNHCR is in "constructive discussions" with the five countries and supports return hubs only if they meet human-rights standards. The International Organization for Migration says it does not take part in state-to-state removal deals but is giving "technical input".

Human Rights Watch's Judith Sunderland said: "History has shown that third-country transfers violate rights and cause suffering." Amnesty International called it a "disgraceful deportation deal" that "repeats mistakes of the past". A coalition of 47 groups, including the International Rescue Committee, warned that people could be moved from lives built in Europe to a country where they have no family.

next: Danish immigration minister Morten Bødskov says the aim is a fully negotiated agreement "within the next few months", with transfers planned to begin in 2027. The UK's earlier Rwanda plan was ruled unlawful by its Supreme Court in 2023 and scrapped in 2024 after four people relocated voluntarily.
summary: Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands announced on 16 November a plan with Rwanda for a "return hub" for people whose asylum claims were rejected and appeals exhausted, aiming to start transfers in 2027. Denmark's prime minister calls it a "game changer" and officials say it will respect international law; Rwanda promises a "second chance" and independent monitoring. UNHCR is in talks, and Human Rights Watch, Amnesty and 47 other groups oppose the plan. No agreement has been signed.
